title: Seeing, not swept
hookLine: the last discourse: training the senses is not closing the eyes but seeing without being swept away

cards: The last discourse in the Middle-Length Sayings opens with a short, slightly awkward conversation.

The Buddha is staying at Kajangala, and a young brahmin named Uttara comes to visit, a student of a teacher called Parasariya. Does your teacher teach the development of the senses? the Buddha asks. Yes, says Uttara.
How? Like this: you don't see forms with the eye, and you don't hear sounds with the ear. Then, the Buddha says, a blind person and a deaf person must be very developed indeed.

teach.b: Uttara goes quiet. The text says he sat silent, shoulders drooping, head down, with nothing to say. The Buddha doesn't press him.
He turns to Ananda and teaches the other way, the development of the senses in his own discipline. When someone sees a form with the eye, something agreeable arises, or disagreeable, or both.
That's going to happen; eyes see.
The trained person understands: this has arisen in me. It's conditioned, it's coarse, it's dependently arisen. But there's something peaceful and fine: equanimity.
Then the reaction fades, and equanimity remains. The pictures are about speed. For the eye, as quickly as someone with good sight might open and shut their eyes.
For the ear, as quickly as a strong man snaps his fingers. For the nose, like raindrops rolling off a sloping lotus leaf without sticking.
For the tongue, like spitting out a bit of saliva gathered on the tip of the tongue. For the body, like a strong man straightening a bent arm.

teach.h: A BLINK, A SNAP, A DROP ON IRON
teach.b: For the mind, like two or three drops of water falling on an iron pan heated all day: they vanish almost at once. The Pali word for the senses here is indriya, the faculties.
So the last discourse of the whole collection lands on something modest. Training isn't shutting the senses down. Liking and disliking will still arise.
The skill is in what happens next: seeing it, and letting it go before it carries you off.

how: Buddhist meditators in several schools practice open-eyed awareness and sense restraint in daily life: noticing liking and disliking as they arise and returning to equanimity, rather than avoiding the world.

o: seeing what arises, and letting it settle
keeping the eyes shut to avoid desire
a vision of the Buddha in meditation

games.q: seeing, not swept: tap the pairs.
p: the young brahmin who fell silent
drops of water on a hot iron pan
faculty, the power of a sense

s: in MN 152 the Buddha says real training means not seeing or hearing
that was Uttara's teacher's view; the Buddha says then the blind and deaf would be developed.
MN 152 is the last discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings
the collection ends with the development of the senses.
the trained person never feels liking or disliking
they still arise. the skill is seeing them and letting them settle quickly.

games.q: the Buddha has just answered Uttara: then the blind and the deaf must be developed. Uttara has no reply. what does the Buddha do?
o: turns to Ananda and teaches the other way.
presses Uttara until he admits he's wrong.
sends Uttara back to his teacher with a message.
games.why: he lets the silence stand and teaches Ananda the noble development of the senses, with Uttara still sitting there to hear it.

practice: Let your gaze rest, eyes open and soft, on whatever is in front of you, and when a liking or a disliking rises, a little pull or push, notice it: this has arisen.
Then let it fall away like water on a hot pan, and come back to just seeing. If a thought drags you off, open and shut your eyes once, and begin again.

wordCard.voice: Seeing. Not closing the eyes, but seeing what arises, liking or disliking, and letting it settle into equanimity before it sweeps you away. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit indriya: faculty, sense power. MN 152 is about developing all six.

carryVoice: Your line: see and stay. The last of the hundred and fifty-two ends with open eyes. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 152, Indriyabhavana Sutta (the development of the faculties)
